title: Signal processing for neural data (Bridge to AI)
text:
CHAPTER 10. RECORDING THE LIVING BRAIN
SECTION 10.4. SIGNAL PROCESSING FOR NEURAL DATA

Why this section

The recording methods of this chapter all produce signals: voltage time series from EEG and electrodes, fluorescence time series from imaging (chapter 12), and BOLD time series from fMRI. Turning these signals into scientific insight, or into control commands for a prosthetic arm, requires signal processing and statistics. This is a dedicated "Bridge to AI" section, and it is also the section most directly connected to the courses a mechatronics student takes: sampling, filtering, Fourier analysis, estimation, and system identification. We will survey the main tools, show how each connects to familiar engineering methods, and see where machine learning enters.

Sampling and digitization

Neural signals are continuous in time and must be sampled. The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem says that to represent a signal without aliasing, the sampling rate must exceed twice the highest frequency present. Spikes have energy up to several kilohertz, so extracellular recordings are typically sampled at 20 to 30 kHz (Neuropixels uses 30 kHz for the action potential band). EEG is typically sampled at 250 Hz to a few kHz. An anti-aliasing low-pass filter is applied before sampling.

Analog-to-digital converters for neural signals need enough resolution to capture microvolt-scale signals in the presence of larger offsets and artifacts. A 16-bit converter with an input range of plus or minus 5 millivolts after amplification has a step size of about 0.15 microvolts referred to input if the gain is matched to that range, which is well below typical noise levels. Designers of implantable systems must also minimize power, because heat dissipated in the brain must stay small; guidance commonly used in the field limits the temperature increase of tissue around implants to about 1 to 2 degrees Celsius. This drives the design of low-power amplifiers and on-chip compression or spike detection.

Filtering

Filters separate signals by frequency. A typical extracellular recording is split into:

- Local field potential: low-pass filtered, for example below 300 Hz.
- Spike band: high-pass or band-pass filtered, for example 300 Hz to 6 kHz.

Filter design matters. Infinite impulse response (IIR) filters such as Butterworth filters are efficient but introduce phase distortion, which can change the shape of spikes or shift the timing of oscillations. Zero-phase filtering (running the filter forward and then backward, as in the common "filtfilt" approach) avoids phase distortion in offline analysis, but it is not causal and cannot be used in real time. For real-time applications such as brain-computer interfaces or closed-loop stimulation, causal filters must be used and their delays accounted for. Filters can also produce artifacts: a sharp transient passing through a filter can create ringing that looks like an oscillation. Several studies have warned that apparent high-frequency oscillations can be produced by filtering sharp spikes.

Spectral analysis

The Fourier transform decomposes a signal into sinusoidal components. For neural data, the power spectral density (PSD) shows how power is distributed across frequencies. Brain signals typically have a "1/f-like" spectrum, with power decreasing with frequency roughly as a power law, with peaks at characteristic rhythms (such as alpha at about 10 Hz). Separating the oscillatory peaks from the aperiodic background is important; tools like FOOOF (now called specparam), developed by Thomas Donoghue, Bradley Voytek, and colleagues in 2020, fit the aperiodic component and the peaks separately. The aperiodic exponent itself has been proposed as a marker of the balance of excitation and inhibition, though this interpretation is debated.

Estimating spectra from finite noisy data requires care. Welch's method averages periodograms from overlapping segments to reduce variance. The multitaper method, introduced by David Thomson in 1982 and popularized in neuroscience by Partha Mitra, Bijan Pesaran, and colleagues, uses several orthogonal tapers (Slepian sequences) to obtain spectral estimates with controlled bias and variance. The Chronux toolbox implemented these methods for neuroscience.

Many neural signals change over time, so time-frequency analysis is used: the short-time Fourier transform (spectrogram) or wavelet transforms, such as convolution with complex Morlet wavelets (a Gaussian-windowed complex sinusoid, closely related to the Gabor function of section 8.2). The analytic signal, obtained using the Hilbert transform, gives instantaneous amplitude and phase of a band-limited signal, used to study phenomena such as phase-amplitude coupling, in which the amplitude of a fast rhythm (gamma) varies with the phase of a slow rhythm (theta). Phase-amplitude coupling has been studied extensively in the hippocampus and cortex, though methodological pitfalls (such as non-sinusoidal waveforms producing spurious coupling) have been pointed out.

Spike trains as point processes

A spike train is a sequence of event times. Mathematically, it is a point process. The simplest model is the homogeneous Poisson process, in which spikes occur randomly with a constant rate r: the number of spikes in a window of length T has a Poisson distribution with mean r*T, and the intervals between spikes (interspike intervals) are exponentially distributed. Real neurons deviate from Poisson behavior, for example because of refractory periods and bursting, but the Poisson model is a useful baseline.

Key quantities for describing spike trains include:

- Firing rate: estimated by counting spikes in bins or by smoothing with a kernel (for example, a Gaussian), producing a continuous rate estimate.
- Peri-stimulus time histogram (PSTH): the average firing rate as a function of time relative to a stimulus, computed across many trials, analogous to the ERP for EEG.
- Tuning curve: the average firing rate as a function of a stimulus parameter (orientation, position, direction of movement).
- Fano factor: the variance of the spike count divided by its mean, which equals 1 for a Poisson process. Cortical neurons often have Fano factors near 1 or somewhat higher, suggesting substantial trial-to-trial variability. Mark Churchland and many colleagues showed in 2010 that the onset of a stimulus tends to reduce variability (lower the Fano factor) across many cortical areas.
- Cross-correlogram: the distribution of spike time differences between two neurons, used to detect synaptic connections or shared input.

Generalized linear models

A powerful framework for modeling spike trains is the generalized linear model (GLM) for point processes, developed for neural data by Emery Brown, Liam Paninski, Jonathan Pillow, Eero Simoncelli, and others in the late 1990s and 2000s. In a Poisson GLM, the instantaneous firing rate of a neuron is

  lambda(t) = exp( k . x(t) + h . y_past(t) + sum over other neurons j of c_j . y_j,past(t) + b )

where x(t) is the recent stimulus, k is a stimulus filter (like a receptive field), y_past(t) is the neuron's own recent spike history, h is a spike-history filter (capturing refractoriness and bursting), y_j,past are the recent spikes of other neurons with coupling filters c_j, and b is a baseline. The exponential nonlinearity ensures positive rates and makes the log-likelihood concave, so fitting is a well-behaved convex optimization problem. Pillow and colleagues used such a model in 2008 to describe the correlated activity of a complete population of primate retinal ganglion cells.

For an engineer, the GLM is a linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade: a linear filter, a static nonlinearity, and a stochastic spike generator. It is like a Wiener or Hammerstein system in system identification, and the same model structure is widely used in machine learning as Poisson regression. The spike-triggered average (the average stimulus preceding a spike), introduced in neuroscience in work going back to the 1960s and 1970s (for example by E. de Boer for auditory nerve fibers), provides an unbiased estimate of the linear filter for white-noise stimuli under some conditions, and is closely related to reverse correlation methods in system identification.

Information theory

Claude Shannon's information theory (1948) has been applied to neural coding since the 1950s. The mutual information between stimulus S and response R,

  I(S;R) = H(R) - H(R|S)

measures how much knowing the response reduces uncertainty about the stimulus (or vice versa), in bits, where H denotes entropy. William Bialek, Fred Rieke, Rob de Ruyter van Steveninck, and David Warland, in the book Spikes: Exploring the Neural Code (1997) and earlier papers, used information theory to show that single neurons in the fly visual system can transmit information at high rates, on the order of a few bits per spike in some conditions, approaching physical limits. Estimating information from limited data is difficult because entropy estimates are biased with small samples, and much methodological work has addressed this.

Dimensionality reduction and population dynamics

With hundreds or thousands of neurons recorded simultaneously, it is natural to ask whether their activity can be described by a smaller number of underlying variables. Dimensionality reduction methods include:

- Principal component analysis (PCA): finds orthogonal directions of maximal variance. Simple and widely used, it is closely related to Oja's Hebbian rule (section 7.1).
- Factor analysis and Gaussian process factor analysis (GPFA, developed by Byron Yu, John Cunningham, Krishna Shenoy, Maneesh Sahani, and colleagues in 2009): separate shared variability from independent noise, and in GPFA, extract smooth latent trajectories in time.
- Demixed PCA (Dmitry Kobak, Christian Machens, and colleagues, 2016): finds components related to specific task variables such as stimulus, decision, and time.
- Nonlinear methods: t-SNE and UMAP for visualization, and methods based on topology. As mentioned in section 9.3, topological data analysis revealed the toroidal structure of grid cell activity.
- Dynamical systems models: linear dynamical systems (state-space models, estimated with the Kalman filter and expectation-maximization), switching linear dynamical systems, and recurrent neural network models such as LFADS (section 10.2). These treat population activity as the output of an underlying dynamical system: dx/dt = f(x, u), y = g(x) + noise, which is exactly the state-space formulation used in control engineering.

A recurring finding is that population activity during a task often lies near a low-dimensional manifold, with dimensionality much smaller than the number of neurons recorded, at least for simple tasks. Peiran Gao and Surya Ganguli argued in 2015 that this low dimensionality may partly reflect the simplicity of the tasks used in experiments, and that more complex tasks may reveal higher-dimensional activity. Carsen Stringer, Marius Pachitariu, and colleagues reported in 2019 that responses of thousands of mouse V1 neurons to thousands of natural images had a high-dimensional structure with a power-law spectrum of variance close to the critical value that keeps the representation smooth. These results are an active area of research.

Decoding

Decoding means estimating stimuli, intentions, or behavior from neural activity. It is used both to ask scientific questions (what information is present in a brain area?) and for applications (brain-computer interfaces). Methods range from:

- Population vector decoding: Apostolos Georgopoulos and colleagues showed in 1982 and 1986 that neurons in monkey motor cortex are broadly tuned to the direction of arm movement, with firing rate varying roughly as the cosine of the angle between the movement direction and the neuron's preferred direction. The direction of movement could be predicted by the "population vector," the sum of each neuron's preferred direction vector weighted by its firing rate change. This simple method was used in early brain-computer interfaces.
- Linear decoders (linear regression, optimal linear estimators, Wiener filters).
- Bayesian decoders, which combine a model of how neurons respond to stimuli (the likelihood) with prior knowledge (the prior) to compute the posterior distribution over stimuli. Kechen Zhang, Iris Ginzburg, Bruce McNaughton, and Terrence Sejnowski used Bayesian decoding in 1998 to reconstruct a rat's position from place cell activity, and similar methods are used to detect replay.
- The Kalman filter, which combines a linear dynamical model of how the decoded variable (such as hand velocity) evolves with a linear model of how neural activity depends on it, optimally estimating the state recursively under Gaussian assumptions. Wei Wu, Michael Black, John Donoghue, and colleagues introduced Kalman filter decoding for motor BCIs in the early 2000s, and variants are widely used (chapter 14).
- Deep learning decoders: recurrent networks, temporal convolutional networks, and transformers, which can capture nonlinear relationships and have achieved high performance in speech decoding from intracranial recordings (chapter 14).

An important caution: decoding accuracy shows that information is present in neural activity, not that the brain uses that information in the same way. A brain area might contain decodable information about a variable simply because it receives copies of signals, without using them.

Causality and connectivity

Neuroscientists often want to know how brain regions influence each other. Methods for estimating "connectivity" from recorded signals include correlation and coherence (functional connectivity), Granger causality (based on whether the past of one signal improves prediction of another, introduced in economics by Clive Granger in 1969), transfer entropy (an information-theoretic generalization), and dynamic causal modeling (DCM, developed by Karl Friston and colleagues in 2003, which fits a biophysical model of interacting regions to data). All of these methods infer statistical dependencies, which may or may not reflect direct causal influences, because unobserved common inputs, measurement noise, and differing signal properties can create spurious dependencies. True causal claims require interventions: stimulation, lesions, or optogenetic manipulation (chapter 12). This distinction between correlation and causation is the same one emphasized in modern causal inference in statistics and machine learning, for example in the work of Judea Pearl.

Summary of the toolbox, in engineering language

- Sampling and anti-aliasing: Nyquist theorem; 20 to 30 kHz for spikes, lower for EEG.
- Filtering: band separation of spikes and LFP; beware phase distortion and ringing artifacts.
- Spectral analysis: PSD, Welch, multitaper, wavelets, Hilbert transform; separate periodic peaks from the aperiodic 1/f background.
- Point processes: Poisson baseline, PSTHs, tuning curves, Fano factors, cross-correlograms.
- Encoding models: linear-nonlinear-Poisson GLMs, spike-triggered averages (system identification).
- Information theory: mutual information between stimulus and response.
- Dimensionality reduction and state-space models: PCA, factor analysis, GPFA, LFADS, Kalman filters.
- Decoding: population vectors, linear filters, Bayesian decoders, Kalman filters, deep networks.
- Connectivity: correlation, coherence, Granger causality, DCM; causal claims need interventions.

Bridge to AI

Nearly every tool in this section is also a machine learning tool: GLMs are Poisson regression, PCA and factor analysis are unsupervised learning, Kalman filters are probabilistic sequential models, and decoders are supervised regressors and classifiers. The flow of ideas goes both ways. Neural data analysis has driven methodological advances, such as point-process GLMs and GPFA, that are useful in other fields. And modern deep learning provides flexible new models, at the risk of reduced interpretability. A growing trend is to train large models on neural data from many animals and sessions, analogous to foundation models in language and vision, and then fine-tune them for specific decoding tasks. Examples include work by Joel Ye, Chethan Pandarinath, and colleagues on neural data transformers and by Mehdi Azabou, Eva Dyer, and colleagues on POYO, reported in 2023. Whether such models will reveal general principles of neural computation, or only predict activity well, is an open question that mirrors debates about interpretability in AI.

Summary

- Neural signals must be sampled above the Nyquist rate and filtered carefully, especially in real-time systems.
- Spectral and time-frequency analysis characterize rhythms and the aperiodic background.
- Spike trains are point processes; Poisson GLMs model them as linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascades.
- Information theory quantifies how much neural responses tell about stimuli.
- Dimensionality reduction and state-space models reveal low-dimensional population dynamics in many tasks.
- Decoders, from population vectors to Kalman filters to deep networks, read out information from neural activity, but decoding does not prove the brain uses that information.
- Connectivity estimates are statistical; causal claims require interventions.
